title: Same Score, Different People
scopeNote: This keeps one domain, the two-level prediction comparison, and the live item-mix control whose crossover shows the tie was a property of the questionnaire. The other two domains, the observation-matching task and the profile-building studio stay in the longer version.
summary: Two fictional people score identically on a broad trait and behave differently. See what the average covered up, then change what the questionnaire asks about and watch the two unchanged people swap places.
learningObjectives: Explain what a broad domain score averages away.
Explain why two people with the same domain score can behave differently in patterned ways.
Compare a facet-level and a domain-level prediction of the same behaviour.
Explain why a domain-level prediction returns the same value for two people with the same score, whatever the behaviour.
Explain how the mix of items in a questionnaire changes which of two unchanged people scores higher.
Say why narrower is not automatically better.
interactionTypes: a judgement about the cause before any evidence is shown
a facet profile table for two people with the same broad score
the same four behaviours predicted twice, from facets and from the domain
a live control over what the questionnaire asks about
two lines crossing at the mix that produced the tie
a guided setting in which the questionnaire tests only one facet
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. The learner is never measured.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Both the facet profile and the two-level prediction are real tables with row and column headers, so no number is available only through the figure. The item mix is a native range input reporting its value in text, and the figure's two lines are labelled by name at their ends rather than distinguished by colour. The chart description gives each person's score at both extremes of the item mix, the crossing point and the current values. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Two invented people, four invented observations and an illustrative 0 to 100 scale. Nobody was measured and no number here is an estimate of anything.
simulationNotes: A person is two facet scores. The domain score is mix * industriousness + (1 - mix) * orderliness, and a behaviour's model-implied tendency is the same weighted average using that behaviour's own weight. Sam and Priya are near mirror images across the facets, so at the halfway mix their domain scores are equal by construction; the page says this is the situation under examination rather than a coincidence. Two results follow and are computed rather than asserted. The domain-level prediction replaces both facet scores with one number, so it necessarily returns the same value for both people on every observation, which is the failure being demonstrated; the facet-level prediction separates them on all four and reverses twice. And because the two trade one facet against the other, moving the item mix moves their scores in opposite directions, crossing at the halfway point and reversing the ranking either side of it. Quoted separations are computed from the rounded values the table displays, so no sentence quotes a gap the reader cannot reproduce by subtracting two cells. Simplifications: two facets rather than five or six; facets that trade off exactly, where real aspects of a domain correlate positively; and behaviour as a linear function with no error term. The facet names come from a published two-aspect account of the Big Five rather than being invented, so the vocabulary learned is one that exists.
readmeTopic: what a broad trait score averages away, and why the tie depended on the questionnaire
